title: Weaning rabbit kits
subtitle: The right age, how to transition kits to solid food, and how to manage the doe.
excerpt: Rabbit kits are weaned between six and eight weeks of age. Early weaning increases stress and digestive disease risk; late weaning reduces the doe's opportunity to recover condition before her next pregnancy. Here is the standard weaning method and what to watch for in the first two weeks after separation.
sourceNotes: RWAF (Rabbit Welfare Association), rabbit breeding and weaning factsheet. British Rabbit Council, breeding guidance. Merck Veterinary Manual, rabbit management (2023).

glossaryTerms.definition: A baby rabbit from birth to weaning. Rabbits are born naked and blind (altricial) and spend the first two to three weeks in the nest box, eyes opening at around 10 days. From three weeks they begin to explore and eat solid food alongside nursing.

content.text: begin eating solid food from three weeks of age while still nursing. By six to eight weeks they are nutritionally independent of the doe, though the doe's milk continues to provide immunity benefits. Weaning at six weeks is standard in commercial production; eight weeks is preferable in small flocks and improves gut health outcomes.

Place a small amount of hay and pellets within reach of the nest box as kits start exploring. Pellets should be the same type the doe is eating. Abrupt changes to feed type during weaning significantly increase the risk of enteritis. Keep the nest box clean and dry; kits have poor thermoregulation before their coat is fully established.
Move the doe to a separate pen rather than moving the kits. Kits remain in their familiar environment, reducing stress.
Leave the kits together as a litter group for at least another two weeks before further separation. Siblings provide warmth and social contact.
Ensure the kits have constant access to hay (the most important element of a rabbit's diet), fresh water, and a consistent pellet supply.
Separate bucks from does by 10 weeks to prevent accidental litters.
Check the doe's mammary glands within 24 hours of weaning. Mild congestion is normal; hard, hot, or painful glands suggest mastitis and need veterinary attention.
Allow the doe a minimum of two weeks rest before rebreeding. Does that are rebred at weaning frequently lose condition over successive litters.
Assess the doe's body condition. A doe with a body condition score below 2.5 (visibly thin) should be given six to eight weeks to recover before her next litter.
